This 68-year-old male with a history of COPD, hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and atrial fibrillation was admitted on 2026-07-14 with an acute exacerbation of his COPD. He presented with worsening shortness of breath, cough, and increased sputum production.

On admission, he was in respiratory distress with a respiratory rate of 28, O2 saturation of 86% on room air. He was commenced on controlled oxygen therapy, intravenous corticosteroids (hydrocortisone), and nebulized bronchodilators (salbutamol and ipratropium). Due to the purulent nature of his sputum and elevated inflammatory markers (CRP 220), he was also started on intravenous antibiotics (doxycycline).

His condition improved steadily over the next 48 hours. His oxygen requirement decreased, and he was weaned off oxygen on day 2 of admission. His respiratory rate settled to 18-20 breaths per minute. He was switched from intravenous to oral steroids (prednisolone) and antibiotics on day 3. His blood glucose levels were monitored closely and required a temporary increase in his long-acting insulin.

He was reviewed by the respiratory team who recommended optimizing his inhaler technique and commencing a long-term home nebulizer service. The patient was deemed medically fit for discharge on 2026-07-16.
